nameStory: The Black-chinned Hummingbird gets its name from the distinctive black throat patch, or 'chin,' that male birds display. This dark coloration creates a striking contrast with the brilliant purple band that sits just below it, making the black portion stand out like a shadowy collar against their tiny necks.
description: The Black-chinned Hummingbird is a tiny, jewel-like bird that's primarily a western species but occasionally shows up as a rare visitor to New England. Males sport a velvety black throat with a stunning purple band at the bottom that flashes like amethyst in sunlight, while females are more subtly colored with pale underparts. Like all hummingbirds, they're incredibly small - about the size of a large bumblebee - and hover at flowers with wings beating so fast they create a soft humming sound. These energetic little birds are built for speed and precision, with needle-like bills perfect for reaching deep into tubular flowers.

idTips.label: Male's purple gorget
idTips.description: Males display an iridescent purple band at the bottom of their black throat that flashes brilliant violet in direct sunlight but can appear completely black in shadow - tilt your head to catch the light just right

idTips.label: Black chin patch
idTips.description: Males have a velvety black throat patch that looks and feels matte compared to the shimmery purple band below it, creating a two-toned effect unique among eastern hummingbirds

idTips.label: Overall coloration
idTips.description: Females and young birds lack the dramatic throat colors and instead show pale grayish-white underparts with subtle green backs that shimmer like metallic paint in good light

idTips.label: Wing sound
idTips.description: Creates a softer, slightly lower-pitched humming sound than Ruby-throated Hummingbirds, though you need a trained ear to detect the difference

idTips.label: Tail pattern
idTips.description: Males show darker tail feathers without the obvious white tips that female Ruby-throated Hummingbirds display when they fan their tails

habitat: In New England, Black-chinned Hummingbirds are extremely rare vagrants that might appear at backyard feeders, flower gardens, or anywhere Ruby-throated Hummingbirds are found. When they do show up, it's typically in suburban areas with plenty of nectar sources like bee balm, cardinal flower, or sugar-water feeders. They seem to favor edges between wooded areas and open spaces, much like their common cousin.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be seen, but any reports would likely come from late April through May when hummingbirds are returning to the region and migration mix-ups are most probable.
seasonality.summer: The most likely time to spot one at feeders or in flower gardens, particularly from June through August when hummingbird activity is at its peak.
seasonality.fall: Possible during early fall migration from August through September, when young birds might wander off course during their first journey south.
seasonality.winter: Virtually impossible to see as these birds migrate to Mexico and cannot survive New England's harsh winters.

funFact: A Black-chinned Hummingbird showing up in New England is like finding a celebrity in your backyard - with only 2 confirmed sightings ever recorded in the region, you're more likely to be struck by lightning than to see one of these western wanderers at your feeder!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with male Ruby-throated Hummingbirds, but the Ruby-throat's gorget is solid ruby-red that flashes like a traffic light, while the Black-chinned shows black with a purple bottom edge. Memory trick: 'Ruby-red versus black-and-purple' - if you see two distinct colors on the throat, think Black-chinned.
contextualKnowledge: The incredibly low observation count (just 2 records) makes this more of a 'holy grail' sighting than a realistic identification challenge for most New England nature lovers. These rare appearances are typically documented by experienced birders and often attract crowds of eager bird watchers hoping to add this western species to their regional life lists.
compareHints: While Ruby-throated Hummingbirds (the only regular hummingbird in New England) have males with solid ruby-red throats that flash like neon signs, Black-chinned males show the distinctive two-toned black and purple throat combination. Female Black-chinned Hummingbirds are nearly identical to female Ruby-throats, making them almost impossible to distinguish in the field without expert knowledge. The purple gorget band on male Black-chinned is the key difference - it creates a stunning layered effect that Ruby-throats simply don't have.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The ruby-throated hummingbird is most closely related to the black-chinned hummingbird of the western United States, but that species has a black throat with purple lower border rather than the all-ruby throat.
